hens_rule_text: Chickens are allowed as a residential accessory use at a rate of 1 chicken per 1,000 sq ft of lot area, rounded down, so a typical 5,000 sq ft lot allows 5 hens; larger lots allow more.
permit_notes: No separate chicken permit found; keeping chickens is allowed by right as a residential accessory use under the zoning code, subject to lot-size formula and coop standards.
setback_notes: Coop setbacks follow the standard accessory-structure rules: 3 ft from side and rear lot lines, 60 ft from the front lot line, and 15 ft from a corner lot line in RS-75/100/150 districts (7 ft in other residential districts). No separate distance-from-neighboring-dwelling rule was found.
coop_rules: Chickens must be kept in a fenced or walled enclosure at all times with a coop on the property; coop maximum height 6 ft, maximum area 125 sq ft, with roughly 4 sq ft of coop space and 10 sq ft of open run per bird.
zoning_notes: Chicken-keeping was added as a residential accessory use by a 2013 zoning amendment; chickens do not count toward the household's general pet limit. Other fowl (ducks, geese, turkeys) fall under separate farm-animal rules requiring a 200 ft setback from neighboring dwellings.
hoa_note: Homeowners associations, deed restrictions and leases can be stricter than city law. Check yours before getting chickens.
code_section: Tampa Code of Ordinances Sec. 27-282.28 (Chickens, accessory use)

sources.name: Tampa Code of Ordinances, Chapter 27 Zoning and Land Development, Sec. 27-282.28 Chickens, Accessory Use

research_notes: Municode is region blocked from this machine, so the lot-size formula, coop specs and setbacks come from WebSearch's quoted extracts of Sec. 27-282.28, which were consistent across two separate searches. The typical hen count of 5 assumes a 5,000 sq ft lot; actual count scales with each property's lot area. Slaughter is not addressed in the sections found.
